segments.text: Good morning, everybody, can the back row hear me okay, great.
I am Marcus, and I want to explain semantic search without a single equation on the slides.
Let us start with a problem we have all had, you search for something and the right answer does not show up.
You typed laptop, but the document says notebook computer, and keyword search has no idea those are related.
Keyword search is matching letters, and it is very good at that, but it does not know what words mean.
Semantic search tries to match meaning instead, and the trick behind it is something called an embedding.
An embedding is just a list of numbers that a model produces for a piece of text.
The model was trained so that texts with similar meanings get lists of numbers that are close together.
So laptop and notebook computer end up near each other, and banana ends up somewhere far away.
I like to picture it as a giant map where every sentence gets a pin.
Searching then becomes: put a pin for my question on the map and look at the nearest pins.
That is really the whole idea, and everything else is engineering around it.
Let us talk about that engineering, because that is where the real decisions are.
First decision, what do you embed, whole documents, paragraphs, or single sentences.
If you embed a whole document, the pin ends up somewhere vague in the middle of everything it covers.
If you embed single sentences, each pin is sharp, but you lose the context around it.
Most teams land on chunks of a paragraph or so, and that is a reasonable place to start.
Second decision, which model makes the embeddings.
We used a Jina embedding model hosted by Elastic, so we did not have to run any GPUs ourselves.
That matters more than people think, because running models yourself is a whole second job.
Third decision, where do the numbers live and how do you search them.
We put them in Elasticsearch with a semantic text field, which embeds the text for you when you index it.
So our app sends plain text, and Elastic calls the model and stores the numbers next to the text.
At query time it embeds the question the same way and finds the nearest neighbors.
Now, the part nobody tells you about is that semantic search is sometimes worse than keyword search.
If someone searches for an error code or a product SKU, exact matching is exactly what they want.
Embeddings will happily return something that feels related but has the wrong number in it.
So for anything with codes, names, or IDs, we combine both kinds of search and merge the results.
That is usually called hybrid search, and it fixed most of our complaints overnight.
Another thing that helped a lot was a reranker, which is a second model that looks at the top results.
The first search is fast and a bit rough, the reranker is slower but much more careful.
You only run it on the top twenty or so hits, so the cost stays reasonable.
Let me show you a small example from our support docs, before and after.
Before, searching for my bill is wrong returned an article about changing your password.
After, it returned the article about disputing a charge, which was what people actually needed.
Nobody used the word dispute in their search, and that is exactly the point.
A few practical tips before I wrap up.
Keep your source of truth in a normal database, and treat the search index as a copy you can rebuild.
Log what people search for and what they click, because that is how you find bad results.
Do not chase the newest embedding model every month, pick one and measure before switching.
And test with real questions from real users, not the ones you invented on a whiteboard.
So, to recap, embeddings are pins on a map, search is finding the nearest pins.
Pick your chunk size, pick a hosted model, keep keywords around for exact things, and add a reranker when you can.
That is it from me, thank you, and let us do some questions.
Yes, in the blue shirt.
So how expensive is this, like does embedding everything cost a lot of money?
Good question, the question is about cost.
Um, for us it was cheaper than I expected, you pay once when you index and then a tiny bit for each query.
The bigger cost was honestly our own time tuning chunk sizes, not the model bill.
Next, over on the left.
What happens when you change the embedding model later, do you have to redo everything?
Yes, you have to re-embed everything, because numbers from two models do not live on the same map.
That is another reason to keep the source of truth in a database, so rebuilding the index is just a script you run.
Hi, does this work for languages other than English?
So, yeah, the model we used is multilingual, and a question in Spanish can find an English answer.
It is not perfect, but it is surprisingly good, and you should test it with your own data.
Last one, I think.
How do you know if the results actually got better and it is not just a feeling?
We kept a list of about a hundred real questions with the answer we expected, and we checked how often it showed up in the top three.
It went from about half to about eight out of ten, which was enough for us to stop arguing about it.
Thank you all, I will be around after if you want to chat.
